claims.claim: Adam Roberts attributes the compelling quality of Le Guin's rendering of Earthsea to a seriousness and an absolute belief in the way she renders the world.
claims.quote: There is a seriousness, an absolute belief

claims.claim: Adam Roberts reads the hero's three names, Duny, Ged and Sparrowhawk, as covering three of the four elements, earth, water and air.
claims.quote: three names covering three of the four elements
claims.page: paragraph on Dun, Ged and sparrowhawk

claims.claim: Sean Guynes says Le Guin's language is at its finest and most artful in The Tombs of Atuan.
claims.source: Sean Guynes, "The Tombs of Atuan: Power, Ideology, and Becoming Uneaten", Reactor, 29 April 2020
claims.quote: language is at its finest, its most artful
claims.page: section beginning 'Le Guin wrote Tombs as a sequel'

claims.claim: Sean Guynes locates Le Guin's finest sentences in The Tombs of Atuan in the plainclothes description of thistle and juniper and frozen reeds by a desert river in midwinter.
claims.quote: her sentences luxuriate in the plainclothes description of thistle and juniper
claims.page: section beginning 'Le Guin wrote Tombs as a sequel'

claims.claim: Le Guin says the sound of characters' and places' names, and the echo-allusions hidden in them, can be intensely expressive.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (2015 revised edition), chapter 1, at Literary Hub
claims.quote: the echo-allusions hidden in them, can be intensely expressive

claims.claim: Stephanie Burt says Le Guin leaves blank spaces for readers to fill in, inviting the reader in and holding them back so that they become co-creators as if listening to an oral tale.
claims.quote: Leaving blank spaces for readers to see how well

claims.claim: Stephanie Burt locates Le Guin's technique of letting the reader fill in the details of a strongly outlined world at the level of the sentence in the first Earthsea trilogy.
claims.quote: letting us fill in the details of her strongly outlined world

claims.claim: Stephanie Burt endorses Plotz's distinction between the prose of Earthsea and the no-detail-left-unturned, purposefully slow-moving prose of The Lord of the Rings.
claims.quote: the no-detail-left-unturned, purposefully-slow-moving Lord of the Rings
claims.page: paragraph beginning 'Plotz may try too hard'

claims.claim: Erin Ramsay says the reassuring sense of fable that pervades A Wizard of Earthsea is lost in The Farthest Shore.
claims.quote: the reassuring sense of fable which pervades

claims.claim: Alessandro Amenta identifies repetitions, paired synonyms and redundancies as typical traits of Le Guin's writing, which the Polish translator tends to remove by periphrasis and by substituting one word for two.
claims.source: Alessandro Amenta, Kwartalnik Neofilologiczny LXX 2/2023, p. 282
claims.quote: which are typical traits of Le Guin's writing

claims.claim: The reviewer on A Novel Review says he could picture almost every scene completely and calls the book incredibly picturesque, which he attributes to Le Guin's writing style.
claims.source: A Novel Review - Book Podcast (video), 11 August 2025
claims.page: closing summary of A Wizard of Earthsea

claims.claim: Mary Anne Mohanraj notes that Le Guin's self-revisions descend to a single word, instancing her bracketed instruction to strike the word probably and replace it with certainly.
claims.source: Mary Anne Mohanraj, Reactor, 1 November 2018, quoting Le Guin's 'Is Gender Necessary? Redux'
claims.quote: Strike the word 'probably' and replace it with 'certainly.'

claims.claim: David Bratman describes Le Guin's essay 'Living in a Work of Art' as a description of the Berkeley house she grew up in, which she presents as beautiful but eminently livable.
A reader commenting on Sean Guynes's Tehanu essay ranks the crystalline prose and storytelling of A Wizard of Earthsea above Tehanu.
claims.source: Reader comment by 'S' on Sean Guynes, 'Tehanu: Le Guin's Return to Earthsea', Reactor, 24 February 2021
claims.quote: the crystalline prose and storytelling of

claims.claim: A reader commenting on Jo Walton's The Other Wind essay says the book is worth reading because one should never turn down a chance at Le Guin's prose.
claims.source: Reader comment on Jo Walton, 'Revising death and dragons: Ursula K. Le Guin's The Other Wind', Reactor, 8 November 2011
claims.quote: one should never turn down a chance at Le Guin's prose
